items.def: all the subjects and topics that are taught in a school, college or course
items.ex: Many educators argue that the national curriculum should include practical life skills such as managing money.

items.def: the process by which more and more people leave the countryside to live in towns and cities
items.ex: Rapid urbanisation has put enormous pressure on housing and public transport in many developing countries.

items.def: involving a lot of sitting and very little physical activity
items.ex: Office workers who lead a sedentary lifestyle are more likely to suffer from back pain and weight gain.

items.def: the ability to question information, judge evidence and reach your own reasoned conclusions
items.ex: Rather than simply memorising facts, students should be taught critical thinking so that they can evaluate what they read online.

items.def: an unfair situation in which some groups in society have more money, power or opportunities than others
items.ex: Unless governments tackle income inequality, the gap between the richest and poorest families will continue to widen.

items.def: the medical condition of being so overweight that it is dangerous to your health
items.ex: Childhood obesity has risen sharply in many countries, largely because of sugary drinks and a lack of exercise.

items.def: learning information by repeating it until you remember it, without necessarily understanding it
items.ex: Education systems that rely heavily on rote learning may produce students who pass exams but struggle to solve real problems.

items.def: the movement of people from one place or country to another, usually to live or work
items.ex: Migration from rural areas to cities is often driven by the hope of finding better-paid jobs.

items.def: intended to stop an illness or problem from happening, rather than treating it afterwards
items.ex: Spending more on preventive healthcare, such as regular check-ups, could save governments money in the long run.
items.fam: prevent (v), prevention (n), preventable (adj), preventative (adj, same meaning)

items.def: the process of judging a student's knowledge, skills or progress, for example through tests, projects or observation
items.ex: Continuous assessment through projects and presentations gives a fairer picture of a student's ability than a single final exam.

items.def: help, especially money, that the government gives to people who are poor, ill or without a job
items.ex: Some people believe that a generous welfare system discourages people from looking for work, while others see it as a vital form of protection.

items.def: the average number of years that a person is expected to live
items.ex: Thanks to better sanitation and medical care, life expectancy has increased dramatically over the past century.

items.def: the money that students pay to a college or university for their teaching
items.ex: Rising tuition fees may discourage talented students from low-income families from applying to university.

items.def: a population in which the proportion of older people is growing compared with younger people
items.ex: An ageing population means that fewer workers will have to support a growing number of retired people.
col: the challenges of an ageing population
items.ar: شيخوخة السكان؛ تزايد نسبة كبار السن

items.def: the state of being healthy, happy and comfortable in your life
items.ex: Spending time outdoors has a positive effect on both physical and mental well-being.

items.def: connected with the practical skills and training needed for a particular job
items.ex: Vocational courses in plumbing or nursing can lead directly to employment, which makes them an attractive alternative to university.

items.def: relating to the structure of a population, such as age, sex or birth rate; as a noun, a particular group within a population
items.ex: Demographic changes, such as falling birth rates, will force many countries to rethink how they fund care for the elderly.

items.def: a situation in which a disease spreads quickly and affects many people in one area at the same time; also any harmful problem that grows fast
items.ex: Some doctors describe the rise in type 2 diabetes as a silent epidemic linked to modern diets.

items.def: the ability to read and write
items.ex: Improving adult literacy can help people find better jobs and take a more active part in their communities.

items.def: treating a person or group unfairly because of their race, sex, age, religion or another characteristic
items.ex: Laws against discrimination in the workplace help to ensure that people are hired on the basis of ability alone.

items.def: a way of eating that includes the right amounts of the different kinds of food needed to stay healthy
items.ex: Schools have a responsibility to teach children what a balanced diet looks like and why it matters.

items.def: copying someone else's words or ideas and presenting them as your own work
items.ex: Universities now use detection software to identify plagiarism in student essays.

items.def: the situation in which men and women have the same rights, opportunities and treatment
items.ex: Achieving gender equality in leadership positions requires changes in both company policy and social attitudes.

items.def: the condition of a person's mind and emotions, including how well they cope with stress
items.ex: Employers are increasingly aware that long working hours can damage their staff's mental health.

items.def: required by law or by a rule, so that you have no choice
items.ex: In my view, physical education should remain compulsory throughout secondary school.

items.def: including people of many different races, religions, languages and traditions
items.ex: Growing up in a multicultural city teaches children to respect customs that differ from their own.

items.def: food that has been changed by industrial methods, often with added salt, sugar, fat or preservatives
items.ex: Busy families often depend on processed food because it is cheap and quick to prepare.

items.def: education at a college or university, after the end of secondary school
items.ex: Access to higher education should depend on academic ability rather than on a family's ability to pay.

items.def: the difference in attitudes, values and behaviour between young people and older people
items.ex: Technology has widened the generation gap, as many grandparents struggle to understand how their grandchildren communicate.

items.def: food that is quick and tasty but contains a lot of fat, sugar or salt and has little nutritional value
items.ex: Banning advertisements for junk food during children's television programmes could help to reduce childhood obesity.

items.def: an official record, such as a degree or certificate, showing that you have passed exams or completed training
items.ex: Many employers now value practical experience as highly as formal qualifications.

items.def: the influence that people of your own age or group have on you to behave in the same way as them
items.ex: Teenagers often start smoking because of peer pressure rather than personal choice.

items.def: lasting for a long time or happening again and again, especially describing an illness
items.ex: Chronic diseases such as diabetes and heart disease place a heavy burden on national health systems.

items.def: describing activities, such as sport, music or clubs, that students do in addition to their normal classes
items.ex: Extracurricular activities like debating help teenagers to build confidence and teamwork skills.

items.def: a person whose behaviour, attitudes or achievements other people, especially young people, admire and copy
items.ex: Famous athletes should remember that they are role models for millions of young fans.
col: a good role model for children

items.def: the health of the population as a whole, and the work done by governments to protect and improve it
items.ex: Smoking bans in public places were introduced mainly to protect public health.

items.def: how well a student does in their studies, usually measured by grades and test results
items.ex: Research suggests that getting enough sleep has a direct impact on students' academic performance.

items.def: a family unit made up of two parents and their children, without grandparents or other relatives living with them
items.ex: In many cities, the nuclear family has replaced the extended family as the most common type of household.
col: the decline of the nuclear family

items.def: the services that look after people's health, such as hospitals, doctors and nurses
items.ex: Some argue that healthcare should be free for everyone, while others believe patients should pay for part of their treatment.

items.def: an amount of money given to a student, usually because of excellent results, to help pay for their education
items.ex: Offering scholarships to gifted students from poor backgrounds is one way to make universities fairer.

items.def: the situation of having no home and often having to sleep outside or in temporary shelters
items.ex: Homelessness is rarely caused by a single factor; job loss, debt and family breakdown often combine.

items.def: the process of giving people a substance, usually by injection, to protect them against a disease
items.ex: Free vaccination programmes have almost eliminated several childhood diseases in many parts of the world.

items.def: a way of studying in which students learn from home or another place, usually online, instead of attending classes in person
items.ex: Distance learning allows working adults to gain a degree without giving up their jobs.

items.def: actions that harm or upset other people in a community, such as vandalism, noise or aggressive behaviour in public
items.ex: Providing youth clubs and sports facilities can reduce anti-social behaviour among bored teenagers.
items.ar: السلوك المخلّ بالنظام العام؛ السلوك المعادي للمجتمع

items.def: the practice of keeping yourself and your surroundings clean in order to prevent illness
items.ex: Simple hygiene measures, such as washing hands with soap, can greatly reduce the spread of infection.

items.def: the idea that people should continue to learn and develop new skills throughout their lives, not only at school
items.ex: As jobs change rapidly, lifelong learning is no longer a luxury but a necessity.

items.def: homes that people on low or average incomes can afford to buy or rent
items.ex: The lack of affordable housing forces many young couples to live with their parents for longer.

items.def: containing the substances your body needs to grow and stay healthy
items.ex: Providing free nutritious lunches at school can improve both pupils' health and their concentration.

items.def: to leave school, college or a course before you have finished it
items.ex: Students who feel that their lessons are irrelevant to their lives are more likely to drop out of school.

items.def: the situation in which too many people live in or use a place
items.ex: Overcrowding in major cities has led to traffic congestion and a sharp rise in housing costs.

items.def: the feeling of confidence and respect that you have for yourself and your abilities
items.ex: Constant comparison with others on social media can seriously damage young people's self-esteem.

items.def: the ability to understand and work with numbers
items.ex: Basic numeracy is essential in everyday life, from managing a household budget to understanding medical advice.

items.def: the process by which people, especially newcomers, become a full part of a society and share its rights and responsibilities
items.ex: Free language classes play a key role in the integration of newcomers into local communities.

items.def: to officially join a school, college or course
items.ex: More adults are choosing to enrol on evening courses so that they can retrain for a new career.

items.def: the number of babies born in a particular period, usually per 1,000 people in a year
items.ex: A declining birth rate may eventually lead to labour shortages and fewer taxpayers.

items.def: the list of topics that will be studied in a particular course or subject
items.ex: Teachers often complain that the syllabus is so full that there is no time left for discussion.

items.def: the feeling of belonging to a group that shares the same culture, language, history or traditions
items.ex: Learning their parents' language helps the children of migrants to preserve their cultural identity.
col: a strong sense of cultural identity

items.def: the practice of training people to obey rules and control their own behaviour; also, a subject of study at university
items.ex: Some parents feel that discipline in schools has become too relaxed in recent decades.

items.def: a fixed and often unfair idea about what a particular type of person or group is like
items.ex: Films and advertisements can reinforce gender stereotypes, for example by showing only women doing housework.

items.def: having a natural ability or intelligence that is much higher than average
items.ex: Gifted children may become bored and badly behaved if their lessons are not challenging enough.

items.def: the state of having very little contact with other people or with the wider community
items.ex: Social isolation among elderly people who live alone can lead to depression and poor physical health.

items.def: involving doing something practically rather than only reading or hearing about it
items.ex: Hands-on experience in a laboratory helps students understand scientific concepts far better than textbooks alone.

items.def: having less money, education or fewer opportunities than most other people in society
items.ex: Free breakfast clubs give children from disadvantaged backgrounds a better start to the school day.

items.def: an exam that is given and marked in the same way for all students, so that results can be compared
items.ex: Critics argue that standardised tests measure only a narrow range of skills and ignore creativity.

items.def: the way in which a child is cared for and taught how to behave by their parents or carers
items.ex: A strict upbringing does not necessarily produce well-behaved adults.

items.def: having a wide range of skills, interests and experiences, not only academic knowledge
items.ex: The aim of education should be to produce well-rounded individuals, not just people who are good at exams.

items.def: the number of crimes committed in a particular area during a particular period
items.ex: Better street lighting and more police patrols are often credited with reducing the crime rate in city centres.
col: a rise in the crime rate

items.def: repeatedly hurting or frightening someone who is weaker, physically or with words, including online
items.ex: Schools should have clear policies to deal with bullying, including cyberbullying that happens outside school hours.

items.def: unpaid work that an offender is ordered to do for the local community instead of going to prison; also voluntary work for the community
items.ex: For minor offences, community service may be more effective than a short prison sentence.
items.ar: خدمة المجتمع (عقوبة بديلة أو عمل تطوعي)

items.def: a school that is paid for by the government and provides free education
items.ex: Parents who send their children to private schools still pay the taxes that fund state schools.

items.def: doing work without being paid, usually to help other people or support a good cause
items.ex: Volunteering at a local charity gives young people valuable experience and a sense of purpose.

items.def: educating children at home, usually by their parents, instead of sending them to school
items.ex: Supporters of home-schooling claim that it allows lessons to match each child's pace and interests.

items.def: the feeling of being accepted as an important part of a group or community
items.ex: Local festivals help residents to develop a sense of belonging to their neighbourhood.

items.def: able to speak two languages equally well, or using two languages
items.ex: Children raised in bilingual homes often find it easier to learn a third language later in life.

items.def: a person who has committed a crime
items.ex: Young offenders should be given education and training so that they do not return to crime.

items.def: a year that a young person takes off between school and university, often to travel, work or volunteer
items.ex: A well-planned gap year can help students mature and choose a university course more wisely.

items.def: the level of success that a student reaches, especially as shown by exam results
items.ex: In most societies there is a clear link between family income and educational attainment.

items.def: the situation in which people from different backgrounds in an area get on well, trust each other and share common values
items.ex: Shared public spaces such as parks and libraries strengthen community cohesion by bringing different groups together.

items.def: poor health caused by not eating enough food or not eating the right kinds of food
items.ex: Malnutrition in early childhood can affect brain development and later performance at school.

items.def: education at college or university level, after primary and secondary school
items.ex: Many governments have expanded tertiary education in the belief that a more educated workforce will strengthen the economy.

items.def: the ability of people to move to a higher social or economic position than the one they were born into
items.ex: Free, high-quality education is one of the most powerful drivers of social mobility.

items.def: the system in the body that protects it against infections and diseases
items.ex: Regular exercise and enough sleep help to keep the immune system strong.

items.def: studying a large amount of information in a very short time just before an exam
items.ex: Last-minute cramming may help students pass a test, but the information is usually forgotten within weeks.
items.ar: الحشو؛ المذاكرة المكثفة في اللحظة الأخيرة

items.def: treated as unimportant and pushed to the edge of society, with little power or influence
items.ex: Policies should be designed to give a voice to marginalised groups, such as people with disabilities.

items.def: describing a disease that spreads easily from one person to another through close contact
items.ex: Children with contagious illnesses should stay at home to avoid infecting their classmates.

items.def: describing a class or group in which students of different levels of ability are taught together
items.ex: In mixed-ability classes, stronger students can deepen their own understanding by helping weaker classmates.
items.ar: متفاوت المستويات (صف يضم طلاباً بقدرات مختلفة)

items.def: the process of helping someone, such as a former prisoner or a person with an addiction, return to a normal, useful life
items.ex: Prisons should focus on rehabilitation rather than punishment if they want to reduce reoffending.

items.def: long life, or the fact of living for a long time
items.ex: Scientists believe that diet, social connections and genetics all contribute to longevity.

items.def: to give students so much help and information that they do not need to think for themselves
items.ex: If teachers spoon-feed students the answers, the students will never learn to solve problems independently.
items.ar: يقدّم المعلومة جاهزة؛ يلقّن دون إشراك المتعلّم في التفكير

items.def: a lack of the basic things people need, such as enough money, food, good housing or education
items.ex: Areas with high levels of deprivation often also have lower life expectancy and more crime.

items.def: systems for providing clean water and safely removing human waste, which protect public health
items.ex: Investing in basic sanitation is one of the most cost-effective ways to prevent disease in poorer regions.

items.def: focused mainly on preparing students to pass exams rather than on wider learning
items.ex: In an exam-oriented system, subjects that are not tested, such as art and music, are often neglected.

items.def: the number of deaths in a particular group or period, usually per 1,000 people
items.ex: Access to clean water and trained midwives has led to a sharp fall in the infant mortality rate in many regions.

items.def: dealing with the whole person or situation, rather than only one part of it
items.ex: A holistic approach to education considers students' emotional and social development as well as their grades.

items.def: something that makes people decide not to do something, especially commit a crime, because of the possible consequences
items.ex: There is little evidence that longer prison sentences act as an effective deterrent.

items.def: professional advice and support given to help people deal with personal or emotional problems
items.ex: Every university should offer free counselling to students who are struggling with stress or anxiety.

items.def: the act of staying away from school without permission
items.ex: Truancy is often a warning sign of deeper problems at home or of bullying at school.
items.ar: التغيّب المتعمَّد عن المدرسة دون إذن

items.def: to commit another crime after being punished for an earlier one
items.ex: Prisoners who learn a trade while serving their sentence are less likely to reoffend after release.

items.def: so serious that it could cause death
items.ex: Allergies that seem mild in childhood can sometimes develop into life-threatening conditions.

items.def: the ability of students to take responsibility for their own learning, for example by setting goals and finding resources
items.ex: University students who lack learner autonomy often struggle when no teacher is checking their progress every day.

items.def: the unwritten rules about how people are expected to behave in a particular society or group
items.ex: Social norms around marriage have changed considerably, with many couples now choosing to marry later in life.

items.def: a mental illness in which a person has an unhealthy relationship with food, for example eating far too little or far too much
items.ex: Images of unrealistically thin models in the media have been linked to eating disorders among teenagers.

items.def: honesty in academic work, such as not cheating and always acknowledging the sources you use
items.ex: The spread of essay-writing websites poses a serious threat to academic integrity.

items.def: an unfair opinion or feeling about a person or group, formed without knowledge or reason
items.ex: Meeting people from other cultures is one of the most effective ways to break down prejudice.

items.def: passed from parents to their children through the genes
items.ex: Although some heart conditions are hereditary, a healthy lifestyle can still greatly reduce the risk.

items.def: a list that ranks schools, universities or other organisations according to their performance
items.ex: Publishing school league tables may push teachers to focus on test results rather than genuine learning.
items.ar: جدول الترتيب (تصنيف المدارس أو الجامعات حسب الأداء)

items.def: describing a group of people who know each other well and support one another
items.ex: In close-knit villages, neighbours often look after each other's children and elderly relatives.

items.def: the ability of bacteria to survive medicines that used to kill them, often caused by the overuse of antibiotics
items.ex: Prescribing antibiotics for minor viral infections contributes to the growing problem of antibiotic resistance.

items.def: extra lessons that parents pay for, usually given to one student or a small group outside school
items.ex: The heavy reliance on private tutoring means that wealthier families can buy their children an advantage.

items.def: a person who has left their own country because they are in danger and is asking another country for official protection
items.ex: Asylum seekers are often unable to work while their applications are being processed, which can leave them isolated.

items.def: breathing in smoke from other people's cigarettes
items.ex: Banning smoking in restaurants protects staff and customers from the dangers of passive smoking.

items.def: a high level of skill or ability in something, especially a language
items.ex: Many universities require international applicants to prove their English proficiency before they can enrol.

items.def: involving or happening between people of different generations
items.ex: Intergenerational projects, in which teenagers teach older people to use smartphones, benefit both groups.

items.def: a tax on drinks or foods that contain a lot of sugar, aimed at reducing how much people consume
items.ex: Supporters of a sugar tax argue that it encourages manufacturers to reduce the sugar content of their products.
col: impose a sugar tax on soft drinks

items.def: to pass knowledge, skills or values on to someone
items.ex: Good teachers do more than impart knowledge; they inspire students to keep learning.

items.def: the separation of people into groups, for example by race, religion, income or sex, so that they live, study or work apart
items.ex: Residential segregation by income can mean that rich and poor children rarely attend the same schools.

items.def: careful about what you eat and how you live so that you stay healthy
items.ex: As consumers become more health-conscious, supermarkets are offering a wider range of low-sugar products.

items.def: to gradually make someone have a feeling, quality or habit
items.ex: Parents and teachers share the responsibility to instil a sense of discipline and respect in children.

items.def: having a lot of money and a comfortable standard of living
items.ex: In affluent societies, people often own more possessions but have no more free time than previous generations.

items.def: the first level of health services that people use, such as family doctors and local clinics
items.ex: Strengthening primary care can reduce pressure on hospital emergency departments.

items.def: the practice of putting students into separate classes or groups according to their level of ability
items.ex: Supporters of ability grouping say it allows teachers to match the pace of each lesson to the class.
items.fam: stream (v) or set (v) pupils by ability; streaming (n, British)
items.ar: تصنيف الطلاب في فصول أو مجموعات حسب مستوى قدراتهم

items.def: the member of a family who earns the money that the family needs to live
items.ex: The traditional idea of the father as the sole breadwinner is becoming less common as more women work full-time.

items.def: the harmful use of alcohol or drugs
items.ex: Young people who grow up in unstable homes are at greater risk of substance abuse.
items.ar: تعاطي المخدرات والكحول؛ إساءة استخدام المواد

items.def: physical punishment, such as hitting, given to children by parents or teachers
items.ex: Corporal punishment has been banned in schools in many countries because it can cause long-term emotional harm.

items.def: placing too much importance on money and possessions
items.ex: Some argue that advertising has made young people more materialistic, so that they measure success by the brands they own.

items.def: a serious illness of the brain, more common in old age, that affects memory and the ability to think clearly
items.ex: As populations age, more families face the challenge of caring for a relative with dementia.

items.def: the average number of students for each teacher in a school or education system
items.ex: Reducing the pupil-teacher ratio allows teachers to give more individual attention to each child.

items.def: the average number of children born to each woman in a country or group
items.ex: As women gain greater access to education and careers, the fertility rate usually declines.

items.def: a gradual rise in the marks given to students over time without a real improvement in the quality of their work
items.ex: Grade inflation makes it difficult for employers to distinguish between excellent and average graduates.

items.def: a system of help, such as government benefits, that protects people from falling into extreme poverty
items.ex: Unemployment benefits provide a safety net for families who suddenly lose their main source of income.

items.def: the desire to do something because you find it interesting or satisfying, not because of a reward
items.ex: Students with strong intrinsic motivation tend to keep studying long after the exam is over.

items.def: connected with the duties and activities of people as citizens of a town or country
items.ex: Teaching civic responsibility at school may encourage young people to vote and take part in local decisions.

items.def: to perform less well than you are capable of, especially at school
items.ex: Bright pupils may underachieve if they feel that their efforts go unnoticed.
items.ar: يقصّر في التحصيل عن مستوى قدراته الحقيقية

items.def: eager to learn about things and to ask questions
items.ex: Young children are naturally inquisitive, but an overly rigid school system can discourage their curiosity.

items.def: a person who starts a university or college course as an adult, usually some years after leaving school
items.ex: Mature students often bring valuable life and work experience to classroom discussions.
col: return to study as a mature student
items.ar: طالب يلتحق بالدراسة في سن متقدمة

items.def: the methods and theory of teaching
items.ex: Modern pedagogy places students at the centre of the learning process rather than treating them as passive listeners.

items.def: the process by which a poorer area of a city changes as wealthier people move in, often pushing prices up so that original residents have to leave
items.ex: While gentrification can revive run-down neighbourhoods, it often forces long-term residents out of the area.
items.ar: تحسين الأحياء الشعبية المصحوب بتهجير سكانها الأصليين (الجنترة)

items.def: a natural tendency to suffer from a particular illness or to behave in a particular way
items.ex: Even people with a genetic predisposition to diabetes can lower their risk by staying active.

items.def: a system in which people gain positions and rewards because of their ability and effort, not their wealth or family
items.ex: A true meritocracy is impossible while children from wealthy families enjoy far better schools.

items.def: to repeat information exactly as you learnt it, without thinking about it or understanding it
items.ex: Exams that reward students for regurgitating textbook facts do little to develop independent thought.
items.ar: يُعيد المعلومات كما حفظها دون فهم؛ يجترّ

items.def: medical care that aims to reduce pain and make life more comfortable for people with a serious illness that cannot be cured
items.ex: Better funding for palliative care would allow more patients to spend their final weeks at home with dignity.

items.def: a strong dislike or fear of people from other countries
items.ex: Economic hardship can fuel xenophobia, as some people blame migrants for the loss of jobs.

items.def: assessment carried out during a course to give students feedback and help them improve, rather than to give a final grade
items.ex: Regular formative assessment allows teachers to identify misunderstandings before they become serious problems.

items.def: protection of a whole population from an infectious disease because a large proportion of people are immune to it
items.ex: Herd immunity protects babies and people with weak immune systems who cannot be vaccinated themselves.

items.def: the number of people who are too young or too old to work compared with the number of people of working age
items.ex: A rising dependency ratio means that each worker's taxes must support a larger number of retired people.

items.def: teaching someone to accept a set of beliefs without questioning them
items.ex: There is a fine line between teaching national values and indoctrination.

items.def: a delay in accepting or a refusal to accept vaccines even when they are available, often because of fear or misinformation
items.ex: Health authorities are working with community leaders to address vaccine hesitancy in areas where few people are vaccinated.

items.def: the process by which a society divides into two groups with completely opposite opinions or very different living conditions
items.ex: Online echo chambers may be contributing to the polarisation of public opinion on social issues.

items.def: favouring a small group of privileged people and treating them as if they deserve special advantages
items.ex: Critics claim that selective schools are elitist because they mostly benefit children whose parents can afford extra tuition.

items.def: a disease, such as heart disease, cancer or diabetes, that is not passed from person to person
items.ex: Non-communicable diseases are now the leading cause of death worldwide, largely because of unhealthy diets and inactivity.

items.def: given only to people whose income and savings are below a certain level
items.ex: Some argue that benefits for pensioners should be means-tested so that wealthy retirees do not receive public money they do not need.

items.def: intended to help students who are below the expected level to improve their basic skills; also intended to correct a problem
items.ex: Many universities now offer remedial classes in academic writing for first-year students.

items.def: making someone physically or mentally very weak, so that they cannot live normally
items.ex: Chronic anxiety can be as debilitating as many physical illnesses, yet it often receives less attention.

items.def: the belief that the needs and freedom of each person are more important than those of the group
items.ex: Growing individualism in modern cities may explain why many people no longer know their neighbours.

items.def: the part of a school's work that looks after students' personal well-being and emotional needs, not only their studies
items.ex: Effective pastoral care can help students cope with problems at home that might otherwise affect their grades.

items.def: the act of deliberately ending the life of a person who is very ill and in pain, usually at their request
items.ex: Euthanasia remains one of the most controversial ethical issues, as it raises difficult questions about the value of life and personal choice.

items.def: the practice of giving money and time to help other people, especially through large donations to good causes
items.ex: Private philanthropy can fund valuable projects, but it should not replace public spending on essential services.

items.def: private tutoring that runs alongside the official school system and closely follows its curriculum
items.ex: In highly competitive societies, shadow education has become so widespread that many parents feel they cannot opt out.
items.ar: التعليم الموازي أو التعليم الظلّي (الدروس الخصوصية الموازية للمدرسة)

items.def: having an illness that cannot be cured and will cause death
items.ex: Some argue that terminally ill patients should have the right to decide how and when their lives end.
items.ar: مصاب بمرض عُضال في مراحله الأخيرة

items.def: involving ordinary people in a community rather than leaders or official organisations
items.ex: A grassroots campaign led by local parents persuaded the council to build safer crossings near the school.

items.def: intended to teach, especially in a formal way that tells people what to think
items.ex: A purely didactic style of teaching, in which the teacher talks and pupils listen, leaves little room for creativity.

items.def: describing an environment or lifestyle that encourages people to eat too much and move too little, causing weight gain
items.ex: Fast-food outlets on every corner and car-dependent suburbs combine to create an obesogenic environment.
items.ar: مُسبِّب للسمنة (بيئة تشجّع على زيادة الوزن)

items.def: crime and bad behaviour committed by young people who are not yet legally adults
items.ex: After-school programmes that keep teenagers busy have been linked to a reduction in juvenile delinquency.

items.def: the tendency to judge people mainly by their formal qualifications rather than by their actual skills
items.ex: Credentialism forces young people to collect ever more certificates simply to compete for jobs that once required none.
items.ar: النزعة إلى تقديس الشهادات (الحكم على الناس بمؤهلاتهم الرسمية)

items.def: a disapproving, informal term for a government that interferes too much in people's personal choices, for example about health
items.ex: Opponents of bans on sugary drinks describe them as an example of the nanny state telling adults how to live.
col: accuse the government of creating a nanny state
items.ar: دولة الوصاية (حكومة تتدخل بإفراط في خيارات الأفراد)

items.def: a punishment in which a court sends someone to prison
items.ex: For non-violent offenders, community-based punishments may be more effective than custodial sentences.

items.def: to fix ideas, principles or habits firmly in someone's mind by repeating them often
items.ex: Schools that inculcate a respect for evidence prepare students well for life in a democratic society.
col: inculcate a sense of responsibility in sb

items.def: describing physical symptoms that are caused or made worse by mental factors such as stress or worry
items.ex: Headaches and stomach pains before exams are often psychosomatic, reflecting the pressure that students feel.
items.ar: نفسي جسدي (أعراض جسدية ذات منشأ نفسي)

items.def: difficult to control and behaving badly
items.ex: Teachers in overcrowded classrooms may spend more time managing unruly pupils than actually teaching.
